mcqs.question: For an internal promotion, why is the raise percentage itself usually harder to negotiate than for an external offer?
options: Companies typically apply a fixed policy band for a given promotion, and exceeding it risks visible internal pay-equity issues among peers, unlike a standalone external offer
Internal promotions never come with any raise at all
HR is legally barred from approving any promotion raise above the previous year's number
Internal transfers always pay less than staying in the same role
mcqs.explanation: A promotion raise sits inside a policy band applied consistently across similar moves, so pushing past it risks visible inequity with peers who received the standard percentage — which is why the percentage itself is far less flexible than an external offer's opening number.

mcqs.question: Why is it worth specifically asking whether a relocation lump sum is "tax-assisted" or "grossed up"?
options: Relocation payments are never taxable under any circumstances
A lump-sum relocation payment is often taxed as ordinary income, so an un-grossed-up amount can net meaningfully less than the stated figure
Asking this question is purely a formality with no financial impact
Tax gross-ups are illegal in most relocation packages
mcqs.explanation: Relocation reimbursements are frequently treated as taxable income, so an $8k lump sum without a gross-up can net closer to $5-6k after tax — a detail most candidates only discover on their first paycheck unless they ask beforehand.

mcqs.question: Why should a visa-sponsored candidate weigh aggressive tactics like bluffing or hard ultimatums more cautiously than a candidate without sponsorship constraints?
options: Visa-sponsored candidates are legally barred from negotiating at all
Sponsoring companies never allow any negotiation whatsoever
Fewer companies sponsor at all, and a job change carries real transfer risk and timeline cost, making the downside of losing the one sponsoring offer higher-stakes than for an unconstrained candidate
Aggressive tactics always work better for sponsored candidates specifically
mcqs.explanation: A visa-sponsored candidate has a narrower set of alternative employers and faces real timeline risk in switching, so a tactic that risks the offer entirely (a bluff, a hard ultimatum) carries a meaningfully higher personal cost than the identical tactic for a candidate without that constraint.

mcqs.question: Why is base salary usually the least flexible lever in a new-grad offer, compared to sign-on bonus or start date?
options: New grads are legally prohibited from negotiating base salary
New-grad base salary is set by government regulation
Sign-on bonuses are always larger than base salary for new grads

Companies often standardize new-grad base pay tightly across a whole cohort to avoid the appearance of unfairness among peers hired together, while sign-on and start date carry less of that visible precedent
mcqs.explanation: A cohort of new grads hired together is highly visible internally, so companies protect base-salary uniformity across that group, while a sign-on bonus or start date shift doesn't create the same visible precedent and retains more per-candidate flexibility.

mcqs.question: What's the most common mistake when applying standard external-hire negotiation tactics to an internal transfer?
options: Pushing hard on a comp number that's structurally capped by policy, while overlooking the scope, title, and timing levers that are actually flexible in an internal move
Not negotiating anything at all in an internal move
Asking about scope and title instead of the number
Requesting the transfer take effect immediately
mcqs.explanation: The comp increase in an internal move is frequently fixed by a policy band regardless of how it's negotiated, while scope, title, and timing relative to the review cycle are the levers that actually have room — treating it like an external negotiation misses where the real flexibility is.

mcqs.question: Why is it worth asking directly whether an internal promotion's raise takes effect at the transfer date or the next review cycle?
options: This timing is always fixed and never worth asking about
Promotions never include any comp change regardless of timing
Some companies default to delaying the raise until the next formal review cycle unless asked, which can mean months of doing the new, higher-scoped job at the old comp level
Asking this question typically cancels the promotion
mcqs.explanation: Without asking, some companies default to aligning the comp change with the next scheduled review rather than the transfer date itself, which can leave a candidate doing higher-scoped work at their old pay for much of a year — a detail worth surfacing explicitly rather than assuming.
